model_annotation: Figure 2 displays the negative log-probabilities of clinically relevant tokens generated by the Mistral-v0.2 model before and after fine-tuning on each of six clinical specialties—Cardio, Gastro, Infect, Neuro, Obstetrics, and Pediatrics—based on data from the S-MedQA dataset. Each specialty is represented by a distinct color-coded bar group, with the left bar in each group showing the average negative log-probability for tokens from that specialty under the baseline model, and the right bar showing the same metric after fine-tuning on that specialty’s data. The y-axis represents the negative log-probability values, with lower values indicating higher token probability (i.e., better model performance). Across all specialties, the right bars (fine-tuned) are consistently shorter than the left bars (baseline), indicating that fine-tuning improves the model’s ability to predict clinically relevant terms specific to each domain. The chart visually supports the paper’s hypothesis that performance gains stem primarily from domain shifting rather than knowledge injection, as the model’s predictions improve most for terms within the fine-tuned specialty, even when those terms appear in other specialties.
